Grand Undertaking

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Taboo or not taboo? Everything you've been dying to know about the serious business of funerals

Unique Selling Point:
We accompany the undertakers from the moment they are called to collect a body from a home or a hospital, on their journey to the mortuary, to the preparation of the body for the funeral, the preparation of the gravesite and the final burial. We also go on a guided tour of the historic Alhambra Theatre, which is now the unique home of Kings & Queens Real Funerals. The three theatres are now three chapels, the backstage area is a coffin showroom and the offices are extremely busy arranging the cross-border repatriation of bodies.

Summary:
We visit 3 distinctly different undertaking businesses:
1. Centurion Funeral Directors
Small family funeral parlour business in Centurion got into this by accident because they had a limo. They themselves suffered three deaths in the family in a short space of time and had to deal with very unsympathetic undertakers. In 2007 they decided to provide a service that would support community families in their hour of need. Their motto is “Compassion & Diversity Personified”.
Now it’s a thriving enterprise with 8 hearses/limos servicing only the Pretoria/Laudium area, specialising in Hindu & Muslim funerals.
Natasha now loves it, loves doing the makeup on the body; finds it meditative and calming, different to the drama of organising catering etc. within 24 hours. We can also go with them to the Rebecca Street Crematorium.

2. AVBOB
Major corporate enterprise with massive HQ in Centurion. It began in Bloemfontein in 1918 in the aftermath of the First World War and the Spanish Flu pandemic. The South African landscape was littered with the makeshift mass graves of those devastated by disease and poverty. In the midst of this devastation, a partially-blind schoolmaster, HH van Rooijen, took it upon himself to create a burial society – a stokvel, if you will. The idea was simple: each human being is entitled to a dignified funeral, at an affordable price. 127 years later, AVBOB still operates as mutual assurance society with members who benefit from the profits. In January they paid out over R13 billion in profits. They now have branches nationwide with 8000 staff members. They offer funeral plans, investment and savings plans that have free funeral benefits. Also, life insurance & legal insurance etc.

3. Kings & Queens
They cater for Zimbabweans, Malawians, Mozambicans etc; anyone who needs to be buried across the border. They handle everything. Many foreign nationals/migrant workers take out funeral policies with them, paying for family here and at home. It began in Orange Grove in 2004, moved to Doornfontein where they have a mortuary. They bought the Alhambra Theatre in 2020 and now have 3 chapels there. Congolese don’t repatriate deceased because of the war; they bury their loved ones here. Usually hold service in the main theatre: extremely noisy; hire DJ’s because they celebrate the life; also hire professional mourners to cry.


Further information:
AVBOB Museum in Bloemfontein holds relics of their rich history; curated by Oom Paulie de Lange. Passionate about the subject, encyclopaedic knowledge. Will take us on the tour.
We will also visit AVBOB’s coffin factory in Bloemfontein supplies the whole country.

Prudence Ndlovu – GM of AVBOB Midrand. She was Manager of Human Resources at HQ but wanted a change from corporate culture. She now runs Midrand branch and loves it. Had to do the AVBOB funeral training, washing bodies etc. but still won’t go into the mortuary alone. 40 years-old, vibrant & passionate. Will give us the tour, tell us all about a day in her life.



Extra Budget Items:
Travel to Bloemfontein (either car hire or flights)
Possible extra shoot day, depending on funerals

Script:


GRAND UNDERTAKING

V/O: There’s something about the dead that captivates the living. The Pere Lachaise cemetery in Paris receives over 3.5 million visitors a year – more than the Kruger National Park.
The biggest television event in broadcast history was Queen Elizabeth the Second’s funeral, watched by an estimated global audience of 4.1 billion viewers. But for most of us, funerals are a more private affair.
Fade to Black

Link: They say that death is Nature’s way of telling you to slow down. But when it comes to funerals it’s all systems go – if you’re an undertaker. So, who are the people that choose this profession, and why do they do it?

Natasha: I actually wanted to be a vet. And then life changed. When we got into the business I still worked. My last job was as a training facilitator at Old Mutual.

Lourensa: So, you went from the corporate world to undertaking; how was that adjustment?

Natasha: I have a passion for being with people and you know, every family is different. Every funeral is different, so we get to have a different job every single day.

V/O: Husband and wife team Silvan and Natasha Pillay run Centurion Funeral Directors in Pretoria. For 17 years they’ve serviced the Indian community of Laudium.

Silvan: We had tragedies in our life. And every time we battled with the service that we received. And then I decide no man, I can do this better. Compared to where we started off out of our community; we’d get one out of every five funerals. Now we get 4 out of every 5, so…

Lourensa: Are there certain time frames that things need to happen in?

Silvan: So, usually with Hindu funerals, Tamil funerals it’s almost an immediate thing. If you pass away in the early hours of the morning, then usually the same day we’ll have the cremation, alternatively the next day. So, we’re quite dependent on the crematoriums, are they available? So, here we are fortunate the crematoriums are working Sunday to Sunday.

V/O: From ashes to ashes, dust to dust, except when it comes to surgical implants. These are some of the things they found in the furnace.

Lourensa: Did it take you long time to get used to working with dead bodies?

Silvan: Actually not; because we did it with a passion, we wanted to do it.
And you know that gut feel that hey, this is meant for me; this I can do. So, I believe I found my calling. I love what I do. I can do it Sunday to Sunday. I got no issue with it.

V/O: When the deceased is female, Natasha assists with washing the body and applying makeup.

Natasha: It’s not the same as you would have because your pores are open when you apply it now. But when you pass away, you cannot put on as much makeup. You have to patch; your strokes are very different, placing on not too much of makeup as well, because it literally stays on top of the skin.

Lourensa: Are there a lot of women in this industry?

Natasha: No, not really. So, in the Hindu undertaker space, I think I’m the first one that’s there. So, culturally, it’s a man’s job. This is normally a very male dominated environment.

V/O: All that is changing. Prudance Ngcongo manages AVBOB Funeral Services in Midrand.

Prudance: So, I am an admitted attorney; I practiced a bit and then went corporate. I have been with Avbob since 2013. I was in the HR department for years.

Lourensa: So, you went from HR to undertaking? Why?

Prudance: I just got to a point where I needed to do something meaningful with my life, something that sort of matters. When I got here, I realised that this is a job that is needed ok; you don’t need another HR manager.

V/O: Prudance had six months of in-house training before crossing over.

Prudance: My training included learning how to do coffining, how to do removals, learning how to take care of the books, learning the systems, how to run the mortuary, how to actually conduct a funeral.

V/O: Early on a Wednesday morning two of her undertakers are preparing to do a removal. That usually means collecting a body from a private home or a hospital.

Nhlakanipho: I like to help; I feel like I’m helping.

V/O: But today they’re collecting the deceased from the Forensic Laboratory in Hillbrow.


V/O: And it seems the body may have been there a while, because the journey back to Midrand is well ventilated.

Prudance: I remember I would get home, and my washing machine is just outside my house. I take off all my clothes and put them in the washing machine and then go upstairs, because I felt like I smelt like death.

Lourensa: What does it smell like?

Prudance: It’s really difficult to explain, but it’s just the smell of death.

V/O: But today she’s quite at home with it.

Prudance: The only thing I have to worry about in the mortuary is, is the fridge working? I mean that’s the one thing that probably keeps me awake at night.

Lourensa: How many bodies can it store?

Prudance: Sixteen, yeah up to sixteen.

Lourensa: And what is the temperature in there right now?

Prudance: So, the temperature has always to be, it cannot be more than 5.

Lourensa: Yeah, it looks like it’s about 3 or 4.

Prudance: Yeah, but it can never start going into minus, because then you start having bodies freezing in there as well. So, you have to check at least three times a day.

V/O: Outside are two refrigerated containers that can take another 32 bodies.

Prudance: So, these containers came here during COVID. The numbers of deaths in the country was just that much that the fridges were not big enough.

V/O: Ironically, Avbob’s origins go back to another pandemic: the Spanish Flu of 1918.

Link: Having lived through the COVID-19 pandemic, it’s difficult for us to imagine the impact of the Spanish Flu on Bloemfontein in 1918. In what became known as Black October over half the city’s population got sick. In just 3 weeks there were more deaths than they’d had in 3 years.

V/O: Schoolteacher HH van Rooijen decided to start a burial society or a stokvel that collected money to assist families with funeral expenses.

Link: There are over a dozen museums in Bloemfontein – from the Afrikaans Literature Museum to the National Museum, to the Anglo-Boer War Museum. Even the ANC has a museum here. But there’s one museum that you won’t find on any tour guide’s itinerary. And even though it’s on Trip Advisor, there are no reviews. Spooky!

Paul: This one we bought the other day from a church in Vredendal.

Lourensa: So, in those years this is how coffins were transported, a horse-drawn hearse?

Paul: Yes, yes, yes.

V/O: Entertaining our morbid fascination is Curator Paul de Lange - from the Chevrolet Caprice to the left-hand drive Cadillac to the world’s biggest collection of model hearses

Paul: 266 of them.

V/O: The museum has eerie artefacts from every decade of the last century, and the most prominent funerals.

Paul: And this is the funeral of Mandela.

Lourensa: Was this also done by Avbob?

Paul: Yes, it was done by Avbob.

Paul: So, this is the mortuary, and these are old fridges that they used to store the bodies in. Do you want to go inside?

Lourensa: No! Not this time.

V/O: It may have started small, but AVBOB is a good example of how the industry has exploded. General Manager Adriaan Bester says they now have 2.7 million members.

Adriaan: We are by far the biggest funeral provider in South Africa. In fact, we believe we’re the biggest funeral provider in the southern hemisphere.

Lourensa: How has this industry changed over the years?

Adriaan: When people pass away now the family expect to have a celebration of that person’s life. They want to have an event that will honour that person, that will be able to live in the memories for a long time; not the horrible day that we had to bury Dad, but you know, a fantastic celebration that we had of his life. And I think that’s probably one of the biggest changes.

Link: When you think about funerals you think about grief, loss and emotional pain. But at the end of the day, it’s still a business, and business is booming.

V/O: From imported steel caskets to a Louis Vuitton wrap to Nguni cowhide with xenon-lit horns, these are designer coffins to die for. And if your loved one never made it to Italy, there’s always the top of the range Renaissance collection – manufactured in Durban with a lifetime guarantee.

Sylvan: This here is the Last Supper printed on the top.

Lourensa: Oh haha! These are lights!

Syvlan: And you get Jesus here on this side.

Prudence: I recently had a client that said look, whatever you do, I want a gold coffin.

Lourensa: Like real gold or just the trimming?

Prudence: No, the whole coffin must be gold.

Silvan: It just gets more elaborate as time goes by. It’s almost like a wedding. Take away your box, you put your bride & groom, there’s your wedding done, you know.

Lourensa: I can see you’ve got a wide variety of hearses?

Silvan: So, when it comes to cars, you have to be competitive with the next guy. And if one guy cuts his car up, you try and cut up one better. You know there’s guys that have Rolls Royce’s that they’ve cut up as well, you know, Phantoms and G Wagons.

Lourensa: What would it cost to do a funeral with this car, this hearse?

Silvan: It all depends on the box. So, we give you this as an option and you get it for free, but it depends what you spend on the casket.

V/O: So, whether you choose to go out with a bang or a whimper, the options are endless. But what about the undertakers themselves?

Prudance: It has changed how I view life.

Natasha: I’ve become more spiritual.

Prudance: You realise that the body is so fragile. Yes, it carries us; it carries your soul and your spirit. But at the end of the day, it just ends here.

Now we get 4 out of every 5, so… Lourensa: Are there certain time frames that things need to happen in? Silvan: So, usually with Hindu funerals, Tamil funerals it’s almost an immediate thing. So, here we are fortunate the crematoriums are working Sunday to Sunday. V/O: From ashes to ashes, dust to dust, except when it comes to surgical implants. These are some of the things they found in the furnace. Lourensa: Did it take you long time to get used to working with dead bodies? Silvan: Actually not; because we did it with a passion, we wanted to do it. And you know that gut feel that hey, this is meant for me; this I can do. So, I believe I found my calling. I love what I do. I can do it Sunday to Sunday. I got no issue with it. V/O: When the deceased is female, Natasha assists with washing the body and applying makeup. Natasha: It’s not the same as you would have because your pores are open when you apply it now. But when you pass away, you cannot put on as much makeup. You have to patch; your strokes are very different, placing on not too much of makeup as well, because it literally stays on top of the skin. Lourensa: Are there a lot of women in this industry? Natasha: No, not really. So, in the Hindu undertaker space, I think I’m the first one that’s there. So, culturally, it’s a man’s job. This is normally a very male dominated environment. V/O: All that is changing. Prudance Ngcongo manages AVBOB Funeral Services in Midrand. Prudance: So, I am an admitted attorney; I practiced a bit and then went corporate. I have been with Avbob since 2013. I was in the HR department for years. Lourensa: So, you went from HR to undertaking? Why? Prudance: I just got to a point where I needed to do something meaningful with my life, something that sort of matters. When I got here, I realised that this is a job that is needed ok; you don’t need another HR manager. V/O: Prudance had six months of in-house training before crossing over. Prudance: My training included learning how to do coffining, how to do removals, learning how to take care of the books, learning the systems, how to run the mortuary, how to actually conduct a funeral. V/O: Early on a Wednesday morning two of her undertakers are preparing to do a removal. That usually means collecting a body from a private home or a hospital. Nhlakanipho: I like to help; I feel like I’m helping. V/O: But today they’re collecting the deceased from the Forensic Laboratory in Hillbrow. V/O: And it seems the body may have been there a while, because the journey back to Midrand is well ventilated. Prudance: I remember I would get home, and my washing machine is just outside my house. I take off all my clothes and put them in the washing machine and then go upstairs, because I felt like I smelt like death. Lourensa: What does it smell like? Prudance: It’s really difficult to explain, but it’s just the smell of death. V/O: But today she’s quite at home with it. Prudance: The only thing I have to worry about in the mortuary is, is the fridge working? I mean that’s the one thing that probably keeps me awake at night. Lourensa: How many bodies can it store? Prudance: Sixteen, yeah up to sixteen. Lourensa: And what is the temperature in there right now? Prudance: So, the temperature has always to be, it cannot be more than 5. Lourensa: Yeah, it looks like it’s about 3 or 4. Prudance: Yeah, but it can never start going into minus, because then you start having bodies freezing in there as well. So, you have to check at least three times a day. V/O: Outside are two refrigerated containers that can take another 32 bodies. Prudance: So, these containers came here during COVID. The numbers of deaths in the country was just that much that the fridges were not big enough. V/O: Ironically, Avbob’s origins go back to another pandemic: the Spanish Flu of 1918. Link: Having lived through the COVID-19 pandemic, it’s difficult for us to imagine the impact of the Spanish Flu on Bloemfontein in 1918. In what became known as Black October over half the city’s population got sick. In just 3 weeks there were more deaths than they’d had in 3 years. V/O: Schoolteacher HH van Rooijen decided to start a burial society or a stokvel that collected money to assist families with funeral expenses. Link: There are over a dozen museums in Bloemfontein – from the Afrikaans Literature Museum to the National Museum, to the Anglo-Boer War Museum. Even the ANC has a museum here. But there’s one museum that you won’t find on any tour guide’s itinerary. And even though it’s on Trip Advisor, there are no reviews. Spooky! Paul: This one we bought the other day from a church in Vredendal. Lourensa: So, in those years this is how coffins were transported, a horse-drawn hearse? Paul: Yes, yes, yes. V/O: Entertaining our morbid fascination is Curator Paul de Lange - from the Chevrolet Caprice to the left-hand drive Cadillac to the world’s biggest collection of model hearses Paul: 266 of them. V/O: The museum has eerie artefacts from every decade of the last century, and the most prominent funerals. Paul: And this is the funeral of Mandela. Lourensa: Was this also done by Avbob? Paul: Yes, it was done by Avbob. Paul: So, this is the mortuary, and these are old fridges that they used to store the bodies in. Do you want to go inside? Lourensa: No! Not this time. V/O: It may have started small, but AVBOB is a good example of how the industry has exploded. General Manager Adriaan Bester says they now have 2.7 million members. Adriaan: We are by far the biggest funeral provider in South Africa. In fact, we believe we’re the biggest funeral provider in the southern hemisphere. Lourensa: How has this industry changed over the years? Adriaan: When people pass away now the family expect to have a celebration of that person’s life. They want to have an event that will honour that person, that will be able to live in the memories for a long time; not the horrible day that we had to bury Dad, but you know, a fantastic celebration that we had of his life. And I think that’s probably one of the biggest changes. Link: When you think about funerals you think about grief, loss and emotional pain. But at the end of the day, it’s still a business, and business is booming. V/O: From imported steel caskets to a Louis Vuitton wrap to Nguni cowhide with xenon-lit horns, these are designer coffins to die for. And if your loved one never made it to Italy, there’s always the top of the range Renaissance collection – manufactured in Durban with a lifetime guarantee. Sylvan: This here is the Last Supper printed on the top. Lourensa: Oh haha! These are lights! Syvlan: And you get Jesus here on this side. Prudence: I recently had a client that said look, whatever you do, I want a gold coffin. Lourensa: Like real gold or just the trimming? Prudence: No, the whole coffin must be gold. Silvan: It just gets more elaborate as time goes by. It’s almost like a wedding. Take away your box, you put your bride & groom, there’s your wedding done, you know. Lourensa: I can see you’ve got a wide variety of hearses? Silvan: So, when it comes to cars, you have to be competitive with the next guy. And if one guy cuts his car up, you try and cut up one better. You know there’s guys that have Rolls Royce’s that they’ve cut up as well, you know, Phantoms and G Wagons. Lourensa: What would it cost to do a funeral with this car, this hearse? Silvan: It all depends on the box. So, we give you this as an option and you get it for free, but it depends what you spend on the casket. V/O: So, whether you choose to go out with a bang or a whimper, the options are endless. But what about the undertakers themselves? Prudance: It has changed how I view life. Natasha: I’ve become more spiritual. Prudance: You realise that the body is so fragile. Yes, it carries us; it carries your soul and your spirit. But at the end of the day, it just ends here.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Taboo or not taboo? Everything you've been dying to know about the serious business of funerals
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We accompany the undertakers from the moment they are called to collect a body from a home or a hospital, on their journey to the mortuary, to the preparation of the body for the funeral, the preparation of the gravesite and the final burial. We also go on a guided tour of the historic Alhambra Theatre, which is now the unique home of Kings & Queens Real Funerals. The three theatres are now three chapels, the backstage area is a coffin showroom and the offices are extremely busy arranging the cross-border repatriation of bodies.
metadata.Summary: We visit 3 distinctly different undertaking businesses: 1. Centurion Funeral Directors Small family funeral parlour business in Centurion got into this by accident because they had a limo. They themselves suffered three deaths in the family in a short space of time and had to deal with very unsympathetic undertakers. In 2007 they decided to provide a service that would support community families in their hour of need. Their motto is “Compassion & Diversity Personified”. Now it’s a thriving enterprise with 8 hearses/limos servicing only the Pretoria/Laudium area, specialising in Hindu & Muslim funerals. Natasha now loves it, loves doing the makeup on the body; finds it meditative and calming, different to the drama of organising catering etc. within 24 hours. We can also go with them to the Rebecca Street Crematorium. 2. AVBOB Major corporate enterprise with massive HQ in Centurion. It began in Bloemfontein in 1918 in the aftermath of the First World War and the Spanish Flu pandemic. The South African landscape was littered with the makeshift mass graves of those devastated by disease and poverty. In the midst of this devastation, a partially-blind schoolmaster, HH van Rooijen, took it upon himself to create a burial society – a stokvel, if you will. The idea was simple: each human being is entitled to a dignified funeral, at an affordable price. 127 years later, AVBOB still operates as mutual assurance society with members who benefit from the profits. In January they paid out over R13 billion in profits. They now have branches nationwide with 8000 staff members. They offer funeral plans, investment and savings plans that have free funeral benefits. Also, life insurance & legal insurance etc. 3. Kings & Queens They cater for Zimbabweans, Malawians, Mozambicans etc; anyone who needs to be buried across the border. They handle everything. Many foreign nationals/migrant workers take out funeral policies with them, paying for family here and at home. It began in Orange Grove in 2004, moved to Doornfontein where they have a mortuary. They bought the Alhambra Theatre in 2020 and now have 3 chapels there. Congolese don’t repatriate deceased because of the war; they bury their loved ones here. Usually hold service in the main theatre: extremely noisy; hire DJ’s because they celebrate the life; also hire professional mourners to cry.
metadata.Further information: AVBOB Museum in Bloemfontein holds relics of their rich history; curated by Oom Paulie de Lange. Passionate about the subject, encyclopaedic knowledge. Will take us on the tour. We will also visit AVBOB’s coffin factory in Bloemfontein supplies the whole country. Prudence Ndlovu – GM of AVBOB Midrand. She was Manager of Human Resources at HQ but wanted a change from corporate culture. She now runs Midrand branch and loves it. Had to do the AVBOB funeral training, washing bodies etc. but still won’t go into the mortuary alone. 40 years-old, vibrant & passionate. Will give us the tour, tell us all about a day in her life.
